title: DEP: Deprecate np.dot when a.ndim >= 2 and b.ndim > 2
body:
Closes #31725

### PR summary

**What problem does this PR solve?**

When `a.ndim >= 2` and `b.ndim > 2`, `np.dot()` and `ndarray.dot()` place `b`'s leading dimensions in the middle of the result shape. For example:

```python
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((4, 3, 5))
np.dot(a, b).shape  # (2, 4, 5) - the 4 ends up in the middle
```

Most users expect either `(2, 5)` (like regular matrix multiplication) or `(4, 2, 5)` (batch dimension at front, like `@`/`matmul`). The interleaved result `(2, 4, 5)` is surprising and rarely intended.

**Ecosystem research:** We checked 9 downstream libraries (scipy, scikit-learn, astropy, pandas, xarray, matplotlib, statsmodels, seaborn, networkx) and found no usage of `np.dot` with a >2D second argument outside of test files. Details posted in #31725.

This PR adds a deprecation warning when `a.ndim >= 2` and `b.ndim > 2`, suggesting `numpy.tensordot(a, b, axes=[-1, -2])` for the same result or `@`/`matmul` for standard batched operations.

**Changes:**
- Created internal `PyArray_MatrixProduct_int()` with `warn_on_interleave` flag, following NumPy's `_int` suffix convention
- All public functions call it directly: `PyArray_MatrixProduct`, `PyArray_MatrixProduct2`, `array_matrixproduct` (np.dot), `array_dot` (ndarray.dot)
- `np.inner` and C extensions call via the public API with `warn=0`
- Warning fires only when `a.ndim >= 2` AND `b.ndim > 2` (actual dimension interleaving)
- Deprecation check runs after shape validation, so shape mismatch raises `ValueError` (not `DeprecationWarning`) even with `-W error`. Also, reusing existing cleanup paths (no redundant conversions).
- Updated `np.dot` docstring with a `.. deprecated:: 2.6` note, and noted the deprecation before the affected example
- Docstring examples still run in the doctest suite: the new warning is added to the doctest ignore list in `numpy/conftest.py` (same as `numpy.fix` and `chararray`), so example output is still checked. Users running the examples still see the warning.
- Added `TestDotDimensionInterleaving` class in `test_deprecations.py` with 7 tests (including shape mismatch priority test)
- Updated `test_dot_errstate` in `test_multiarray.py` and masked array tests in `test_core.py` and `test_extras.py` to expect the warning
- Added release note (`32759.deprecation.rst`)

**Why an internal wrapper?**

The deprecation check was initially placed in `PyArray_MatrixProduct2()`, but `np.inner()` also calls this shared function and should not trigger the warning. Rather than duplicating the matrix product logic, we created an internal implementation with a flag parameter. This avoids code duplication while keeping the warning scoped to `np.dot`/`ndarray.dot` only.

**Lesson learned:** Running `spin test` (the full test suite) locally before pushing catches failures earlier, rather than discovering them in CI. Additionally, running the doctest suite (`spin test -- --doctest-modules --doctest-only-doctests=true --doctest-collect=api`) catches failures in docstring examples that unit tests miss.

#### AI Disclosure

AI assisted with codebase navigation, identifying NumPy conventions for deprecation warnings and tests, and drafting code and documentation. All changes were reviewed and tested locally before submitting.

title: BUG: fix result mask placement in np.ma.isin and np.ma.in1d (gh-19877)
body:
`numpy.ma.in1d` currently handles masks incorrectly when the first input
contains masked elements. The membership values themselves are correct, but
the mask on the result can be applied to the wrong positions.

This change makes the membership check operate on the underlying data while
preserving the mask positions from the first input. Masked values in the
second input are also excluded from the set of values used for the membership
check.

`setdiff1d`, which also relies on `in1d`, is updated accordingly so that
masked elements are preserved correctly in its result.

Closes #19877

## Why was this issue selected?

I picked this issue because it is a relatively small but concrete bug in
`numpy.ma` behavior, and it gave me an opportunity to understand how masked
arrays are handled internally. Fixing it also helps make the behavior of
`in1d`/`isin` more consistent when masked data is involved.

## First-time contributor

Hi, I'm Md Imam Hossain. I'm currently studying B.Tech CSE AILML and
mostly use Python for [ML/data analysis/scientific computing/etc.]. I have
been using NumPy as part of my Python work, and this is my first contribution
to the NumPy project.

## Tests

Added a regression test covering masked input to ensure that:

- membership is determined from the underlying data;
- masked positions in the first argument remain masked in the result; and
- masked values in the second argument are not treated as values to match.

The relevant `numpy.ma` tests were run to check for regressions.

title: DOC: add table of which operations return views or copies
body:
### PR summary
<!-- Please take some time to make it easier for us to review
your pull request (PR). Describe the PR using the questions below as guidance.

Please note that non-maintainers may only have 2 non-draft PRs open for review at a
time.

-->
- What problem does this PR solve? Link any relevant issues and PRs.

This PR is related to [issue 20112](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/20112).
The code aims to document the numpy operations that return views vs copies.
I added a comment to the issue asking some feedback on the approach, I have not heard back so I am submitting in this PR a first version of the documentation to get some feedback and understand if the methodology (explained below) makes sense.

As I was trying to verify the behaviour of different operations I realised that there are some interesting cases which have a different return type depending on the input. I think for those it would be worth adding a snippet of the code showing what happens with different inputs. 
This PR only adds a section in [Copies and views](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.copies.html) with the return types without any code.

#### How each operation was classified

Every entry was checked against a build of current `main`, not taken from the docstrings. Each operation runs on a sample array `x` and produces `y`:

```python
if y is x:                    # the operation handed back its input
    outcome = "same"
elif np.shares_memory(x, y):  # a different array over the same memory
    outcome = "view"
else:
    outcome = "copy"
```

`same` and `view` are both reported as "View", since neither copies data.

I initially used `y.base` as the documentation says: 
"_The `base` attribute of the ndarray makes it easy to tell if an array is a view or a copy. The base attribute of a view returns the original array while it returns None for a copy."_

While testing different cases I saw that checking `.base` might still return `False` when the return is a view that can edit the original array. For example:

```python
x = np.arange(24).reshape(4, 6).copy()

y = x.T.reshape(-1)        # reshape cannot view a transposed array, so it copies
y.base is None             # False: .base says view
np.shares_memory(x, y)     # False: it is a copy

z = np.asarray(x)          # returns x itself, nothing copied
z.base is None             # True: .base says copy
np.shares_memory(x, z)     # True: it is x
```
That is why I decided to use `np.shares_memory`. `.base` was only used for empty results since `np.shares_memory` is `False` even for a view of an empty array.
With this in mind, it might be worth editing [this section ](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.copies.html#how-to-tell-if-the-array-is-a-view-or-a-copy)of the docs too. Let me know if you agree with the approach.

A mix of outcomes is reported as "View or copy", with the note saying what determines it:

- Why are you interested in working on this PR?

Was looking at different open issues an since this is my first contribution I wanted to start with a doc change to get some experience. This issue stood out since understanding which operations share memory with the original array can avoid some unpleasant surprised and clarifies what your code is actually editing.

- How does the proposed change help you?

I am part of the 2026 Sustain cohort, would like to keep contributing to open source, especially numpy-financial.

## PR summary

TL;DR
This fixes the UBSan-reported undefined shift in `_rational_tests.c` by using NumPy's existing minimum-value constant instead. The corresponding UBSan suppressions for arm64 and x86_64 are removed as they are no longer needed. There is no intended API or behavior change.

Previously, `safe_neg()` used `(npy_int32)1 << 31` to construct the minimum 32-bit signed value, which UBSan reports as undefined behavior. The check now uses `NPY_MIN_INT32`.

This addresses the `_rational_tests.c` `shift-base` item in the UBSan cleanup tracker.

Related:
- Tracking issue: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29524
- Prior related UBSan shift cleanup: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/29539

title: MAINT: silence `invalid` warning for `np.exp(complex(np.nan, np.nan))` and such
body:
### PR summary
On some platforms, `np.exp` with complex NaN input produce `invalid` warnings. Based on the behavior of other ufuncs and other precedent (e.g. gh-12236, gh-15988, gh-32602, and now gh-32706), I don't think this is desired anymore. This silences the warnings by providing an early return path.
